title: Emergency hygiene, toilets and waste
h1: Emergency hygiene, handwashing, toilets and waste when services fail
dek: Handwashing without a tap, a toilet when the sewer is down, and what to do with the waste. The CDC, a state health department and a university extension describe it plainly, and disagree on one point we flag.
description: How to wash hands, set up a bag or twin-bucket toilet and handle waste when water and sewer service fail, from the CDC, Washington DOH and OSU Extension.
recheck: If CDC revises its hygiene or septic pages (the septic page was revised in August 2026), or when local waste-disposal guidance is checked; otherwise at the next quarterly source sweep.

source_use.cdc-hygiene-emergency: Handwashing for at least 20 seconds; when boiled or disinfected water is recommended; temporary jug station; sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol and its limits; bathing, teeth, wound care and Vibrio; diaper fact sheets pointer.
source_use.health-cdc-septic: Limit flushing and water use in an emergency; flush as little as possible or use a temporary toilet; do not pump a flooded septic tank more than halfway; signs of failure; avoid sewage-contaminated floodwater; do not drink well water until known safe; pre-flood steps for septic households.
source_use.health-cdc-sanitation-archive: Archived emergency-response comparison of toilet options and their constraints; handwashing at every sanitation facility; containing waste reduces disease spread (cited as general principle only).
source_use.health-wadoh-toilet: Three toilet options; the bag-lined bowl steps; the bucket option; cat-hole conditions; wipes and sanitizer if no running water; bagging non-biodegradable items; suggested disposal in the garbage (the point on which it disagrees with OSU).
source_use.health-osu-sanitation: Toilet blindness; fecal-oral disease risk; twin-bucket set-up, use and emptying; avoid toilets even if home pipes seem fine; turn off household water; handwashing station design; CDC key handwashing times as listed; sanitizer caveats; diapers, menstrual products and mobility; supply list; do not put human waste in normal garbage.
source_use.health-cdc-power-outage: Safe water for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene is bottled, boiled or treated.
source_use.health-ready-kit: One gallon per person per day counts for drinking and sanitation; moist towelettes, garbage bags and ties; soap, sanitizer, diapers, feminine and hygiene supplies.
